title: Ultra log-concavity for increasing families generated by singletons and pairs
shortTitle: Dependent sets of a graph are ultra log-concave
oneLine: For any graph, the fraction of k-vertex sets that contain an edge forms a log-concave sequence in k, even with vertex weights, proving Xie and Xu's Conjecture 4.1; witnesses of size three already break it.
abstract: Pick a graph on n vertices and call a set of vertices dependent if it contains at least one edge. Let d_k count the dependent k-vertex sets. Horrocks (2002) proved that d_k is log-concave. Xie and Xu (Electronic Journal of Combinatorics, 2026) conjectured the stronger ultra log-concave form, their Conjecture 4.1: d_k/C(n,k) is log-concave, so the size of a uniformly random dependent set is at least as concentrated as a binomial distribution. This candidate proves that conjecture in a weighted form, for every increasing family generated by singletons and pairs (graphs with loops) and arbitrary nonnegative element weights: k(n−k)A_k² ≥ (k+1)(n−k+1)A_{k−1}A_{k+1}. The proof first shows that the binomially normalised number of k-sets S with both S and its complement dependent is symmetric and unimodal, a strengthening of a 2000 theorem of Horrocks, using a marked-downset lemma derived from Katona's shadow theorem and a critical-element double count; the property survives conditioning, and the Kahn–Neiman antipodal-pairs criterion converts it into ultra log-concavity. The paper also proves a weighted form of Xie and Xu's Conjecture 4.4 for additive 2-matroids of rank at most four or on at most seven elements (the general conjecture remains open), shows that witnesses of size three break the theorem (counts (0,1,4,10,5,1) give 96 < 120), and derives ultra log-concavity of noncover-complex face numbers and a variance bound for Bernoulli variables conditioned to hit an edge. AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate; no external peer review, independent reproduction or formal verification is claimed.

keyResults: Main theorem (Theorem 1.1): for every increasing family generated by singletons and pairs and all nonnegative weights, k(n−k)A_k² ≥ (k+1)(n−k+1)A_{k−1}A_{k+1}; with unit weights this is Xie–Xu Conjecture 4.1 for the dependent-set counts d_k of every graph.

Two-colouring theorem (Theorem 1.2): the number b_k of k-sets S with S and its complement both dependent, divided by C(n,k), is symmetric and unimodal; this strengthens Horrocks's 2000 unimodality theorem and survives fixing any coordinates.

2-matroids (Section 6): a weighted form of Xie–Xu Conjecture 4.4 holds for additive 2-matroids of rank at most four or on at most seven elements, and the first three inequalities hold in any rank; the general conjecture remains open, with an explicit eight-element obstruction to the method.

Sharpness (Section 5.3): witnesses of size three break the theorem; a five-element family with counts (0,1,4,10,5,1) gives 96 < 120, two disjoint triples with weights (1,M,M,3,3,3) fail exactly for M ≥ 44, and six elements is the minimum for a uniform-triple counterexample.

Consequences (Section 5): ultra log-concave face numbers for noncover complexes, and Var(K) ≤ m(1 − m/n) for the number K of successes among independent Bernoulli variables conditioned to contain an edge, with mean m.

narration: Do the edge-containing sets of a graph spread out like coin tosses? An Evidence Press briefing. Take any network of points joined by links, what mathematicians call a graph. Pick some of its points, and call your choice dependent if it includes both ends of at least one link. For each size k, count the dependent choices of k points. In 2002 David Horrocks proved that these counts are log-concave: they rise and then fall smoothly, with no second hump. In 2026 Yan-Ting Xie and Shou-Jun Xu conjectured something stronger. Divide each count by the total number of ways to choose k points, so that you get the fraction of k-point choices that are dependent. They conjectured that this sequence of fractions is still log-concave. This is called ultra log-concavity, and it means that the size of a random dependent choice is at least as tightly concentrated as the number of heads in a run of coin tosses. They had proved it only for two special families of graphs. This paper proves it for every graph, and more: each point may carry a weight, and single points may also count as dependent on their own. The key step is a new fact about splitting the points into two groups so that each group contains a link: after the same division, the number of such splits rises and falls symmetrically. A classical counting theorem of Katona and a criterion of Kahn and Neiman then finish the argument. The paper shows the condition is sharp: if a dependent choice must contain three linked points instead of two, the property can fail, with ninety-six falling short of one hundred and twenty in a five-point example. It also settles a broader conjecture of Xie and Xu for small cases, while the general case remains open. A practical consequence is a variance bound for random sets conditioned to contain a link. Computer checks of all small cases support the proofs but are not the proofs. This is an anonymous, AI-assisted, unrefereed candidate, not peer reviewed or independently reproduced. Published on the fourth of November twenty twenty-six, its paper and code are linked from the Evidence Press release page. This briefing uses an AI-generated voice and is not additional scientific evidence.

relatedWorks.citation: Xie and Xu (2026). Ultra log-concavity and real-rootedness of dependence polynomials. The Electronic Journal of Combinatorics 33(4), P4.9. States Conjecture 4.1, proved here in weighted form, and Conjecture 4.4 on 2-matroids, proved here for rank at most four or at most seven elements.

Horrocks (2002). The numbers of dependent k-sets in a graph are log concave. Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series B. Proves ordinary log-concavity of the counts (with an extra +p_k term), not the ultra form. Read in full for version 0.2.0: its proof sorts pairs of sets by intersection and union and reduces to doubly dependent counts, a precursor of this paper's method that is now credited.

Kahn and Neiman (2011). A strong log-concavity property for measures on Boolean algebras. Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A. The antipodal-pairs criterion used to convert the two-colouring theorem into ultra log-concavity.
Frankl (2016). Linear independence, a unifying approach to shadow theorems. European Journal of Combinatorics. Source used for the statement of Katona's intersection-shadow theorem.
Liggett (1997). Ultra logconcave sequences and negative dependence. Journal of Combinatorial Theory, Series A. Background on ultra log-concavity and its closure under convolution.

Anari, Liu, Oveis Gharan and Vinzant (2024). Log-concave polynomials III: Mason's ultra-log-concavity conjecture for independent sets of matroids. Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society. The matroid analogue for independent sets.
Brändén and Huh (2020). Lorentzian polynomials. Annals of Mathematics. A second proof of Mason's conjecture; the paper explains why this route does not apply directly to dependent sets.

corrections.summary: Version 0.2.0-candidate corrects the prior-art record. Version 0.1.0-candidate credited Horrocks (2002) from its abstract only; the paper has now been read in full and compared theorem by theorem.
corrections.detail: Horrocks proves p_k^2 >= p_(k-1)p_(k+1) + p_k for every graph. This is unweighted, has no binomial normalisation and does not imply ultra log-concavity. His Lemma 2.1 sorts pairs of sets by intersection and union and reduces to doubly dependent counts, with neighbours acting as forced witnesses. That is a direct precursor of this paper's conditioning and antipodal-pairs route, and it is now credited in Section 1 of the manuscript. The binomially normalised two-colouring theorem, the marked-downset lemma and the critical-element count are not in his paper. No theorem, proof or computation changed. Version 0.1.0-candidate (DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23935650, tag v0.1.0-candidate) remains unchanged.
